Chronology 4 — Abraham

The Bible's text — what is actually said

  • Gen 12–25: the call, the covenant, circumcision. Ishmael (by Hagar) is blessed and made a great nation, but the covenant runs through Isaac (Gen 17:19–21).
  • The binding (Gen 22): "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love…"; the three-day journey; "God will provide the lamb"; the knife stayed; the ram caught in the thicket; the oath-blessing "in your offspring all nations shall be blessed" (22:16–18). The son is named, four times, explicitly — Isaac.
  • NT use: Abraham's faith "reckoned as righteousness" before the law and circumcision (Rom 4; Gen 15:6) — the keystone of the justification-by-faith argument; the offering as foreshadowing (Heb 11:17–19); faith proven by works (James 2:21–23); the Hagar/Sarah allegory (Gal 4).

The Qur'an's text — what is actually said

  • Natural-theology scene: the young Ibrahim reasons from a star, the moon, the sun ("I love not those that set") to the Creator (Q 6:74–79) — a rare explicit argument for monotheism, not mere assertion.
  • He shatters the idols and survives the fire (Q 21:51–70; 37:97).
  • The offering (Q 37:100–113): the dream — "O my son, I see in a dream that I sacrifice you; what do you think?"; the son's submission — "do as you are commanded; you will find me patient"; the ransom of "a great sacrifice" (dhibḥin ʿaẓīm) — the basis of ʿId al-Aḍḥa. The son is unnamed at the offering ("a forbearing boy", ghulām ḥalīm).
  • Ibrahim and Ismaʿil raise the foundations of the Kaʿba (Q 2:127); Ibrahim settles offspring in a "barren valley" (Q 14:37 — read as Mecca) and prays "raise among them a messenger" (Q 2:129 — read as Muhammad). Ibrahim is a ḥanīf, "neither Jew nor Christian" but a muslim (Q 3:67).

Collision

  1. Who was offered? The Bible is explicit (Isaac). The Qurʾan is silent at the offering; the "Ishmael" answer is supplied by tafsīr.
  2. Covenant line: Bible → Isaac/Israel; Qurʾan → Ibrahim as the proto-muslim, the Kaʿba/Hajj/Mecca origin, and the prayed-for messenger (no biblical parallel).
  3. "Abraham was a muslim" (Q 3:67) vs. Abraham the father of Israel and of justifying faith (Gen; Rom 4).

The strongest Muslim textual argument — stated fairly

Honesty (and symmetry) require giving the best Muslim case, not a strawman:

  • In Q 37 the *good news of Isaac (37:112) comes after the sacrifice narrative (37:101–107). The internal argument: the son already born and offered must therefore be the earlier son — Ishmael — with Isaac announced as a subsequent* reward. This is a non-trivial ordering argument from the text itself, not mere tradition.
  • The counter-weights: the Qurʾan still never names the offered son; several major early Muslim authorities held it was Isaac; and the Bible is fourfold explicit (Isaac) including the loaded "your only son" (true of Isaac as the covenant son; true of Ishmael only before Isaac's birth).

Net: the Qurʾan is genuinely ambiguous with a real but inconclusive internal argument; the Bible is explicit. This is more balanced than "pure tradition vs. text" — but the explicitness still lies with the Bible.

Arbiter verdict — Abraham

Present. Shared patriarch and monotheistic exemplar. Bible: explicit Isaac, covenant through Isaac. Qur'an: unnamed son, Ibrahim as universal hanif, Kaaba foundation.

Weigh.

  • Textual explicitness: the Bible names the son four times (Isaac); the Qurʾan never names him at the offering. The Muslim case is not pure tradition — the Q 37 ordering argument is real — but it is inconclusive, and early Muslim authorities were themselves split.
  • Unattested salvation-history claims, both sides: the Kaʿba's Abrahamic construction, Mecca, and "Abraham was a muslim" have no pre-Islamic or biblical corroboration; the covenant-through-Isaac/Israel reading is likewise a theological claim. Both are faith claims, not history (Methodology §1).
  • Not a corruption proof either way: differing emphases here do not, by themselves, prove tampering of either text.

Judge. On "which text actually states who was offered?": the Bible wins on explicitness (Isaac, fourfold, with "your only son"); the Qurʾan is deliberately ambiguous and the Ishmael reading, while supported by a legitimate internal ordering argument, is not decisively the Qurʾan's own statement. On the theological repurposing (proto-muslim, Kaʿba, the prayed-for messenger): these are unfalsifiable faith claims with no external support — recorded as claims, not data (out of remit). Net: a measured point to textual precision on the Bible's side, with the Muslim ordering argument fairly credited as more than tradition — and a flag that both scriptures here build large, unverifiable salvation-history on the same patriarch.
